meldungen.titel: Consulting Deep Dive, part 6: Oliver Wyman and Kearney, the specialists who win where MBB is merely good
meldungen.text:
Below McKinsey, BCG and Bain sits a tier of firms whose brand is narrower but, in their home turf, every bit as strong. Two of them are worth a close look for you: Oliver Wyman, the house of financial services, and Kearney, the house of operations and procurement. Choosing either is less a step down than a bet on a specialism, and that bet shapes your exits for a decade.

Oliver Wyman belongs to Marsh McLennan, the insurance broking and advisory group that also owns Mercer and NERA Economic Consulting. Headcount estimates range from roughly 5,500 to about 7,000 depending on the source, spread across some 70 cities in 30 countries. Its flagship is financial services: strategy, risk, regulation and transformation work for banks, insurers and asset managers. Only this week it agreed to buy Synpulse, a Swiss consultancy specialising in technology for financial institutions, to deepen its AI practice, which tells you where the firm sees its next decade.

That focus defines the exits. Career guides and forum accounts consistently describe financial services as the widest funnel: senior strategy, risk and corporate development roles at banks, insurers and asset managers, then corporate strategy at large companies and value creation teams at private equity funds. One guide puts it pointedly: Oliver Wyman opens doors in financial services that most consultancies, MBB included, cannot, but demands more deliberate effort than MBB for generalist exits such as large-cap private equity. Private equity is achievable, particularly from the financial services practice, but it is not the default path.

Kearney, spun out of the old A.T. Kearney, is built around operations. Its own site says procurement "isn't a side offering. It's our core", and Management Consulted describes its strongest reputation as operations, procurement and supply chain transformation. Juniors start in a general practice across industries and functions and typically choose a practice only at senior associate or manager level, so you are not locked in on day one. Current postings show where it is heading: its Digital and Analytics practice now recruits for "agentic procurement transformation", AI agents running purchasing processes.

Kearney's typical exits follow from that profile: corporate strategy and transformation roles, procurement and cost leadership, private equity portfolio operations (the people who fix companies after the deal, rather than those who pick them), and graduate programmes. One coaching site sums up the trade-off: Kearney trails MBB on brand pull and access to private equity deal teams, matches it in corporate strategy at manager and director level, and beats it in operations, supply chain and procurement leadership. A word of caution: none of the sources offers hard placement statistics, and most come from interview-prep firms, so treat the patterns as directional.

The long-term arithmetic is simple. Oliver Wyman is the natural springboard if you can picture yourself as a bank's head of strategy, a chief risk officer or an investor in fintech; Kearney if you see yourself as COO, head of procurement or an operating partner at a buyout fund. Neither is ideal if your single goal is a large-cap private equity deal team; there, MBB still has the edge.

meldungen.titel: Booth, Columbia and Kellogg lead the M7 in Big Four alumni
meldungen.text:
Which elite business schools send the most people through Deloitte, PwC, EY and KPMG? According to a new data analysis by Poets and Quants, nearly one in ten Chicago Booth alumni has worked at one of the Big Four at some point in their career, roughly twice the share at Harvard Business School or Stanford's Graduate School of Business. Columbia and Kellogg complete the leading trio among the so-called M7, the seven most prestigious American MBA programmes.

The finding sits well with an earlier Poets and Quants profile of the M7, which noted that Booth and Kellogg send most of their MBAs into consulting. The full breakdown by firm and school was not accessible this morning, so the figures above are limited to the publication's own summary.

meldungen.titel: From student to lecturer in one leap: a Kellogg MBA now teaches Claude Code
meldungen.text:
Pablo Landa, a member of Kellogg's MBA Class of 2026, has crossed to the other side of the lectern. He now co-teaches Kellogg's Applied AI Lab, the course he once took as a student, and runs sessions on Claude Code and on building skills for AI agents, Poets and Quants reports.

The Applied AI Lab is a hands-on course in which MBA students build and ship working AI products for partner companies; according to Kellogg, students have built 28 such products over the past two years, and the lab has become a formal ten-week course co-taught by Landa and Benjamin Grant, a clinical associate professor of operations. Kellogg's faculty profile notes that Landa, as a "Claude Builder" with Anthropic, drove the adoption of Claude across campus with workshops and hackathons, co-led the Kellogg AI Club and received a Dean's Distinguished Service Award this year.

The story illustrates how quickly practical AI fluency has become a currency at business schools: a skill picked up during the degree turned into a teaching post before graduation.

meldungen.titel: The IPO pop lasted a day: Anthropic slides towards its offering price as banks exercise the greenshoe
meldungen.text:
Anthropic's debut euphoria proved short-lived. On its second day as a listed company the stock surrendered most of its first-day gains: almost an hour after the opening bell it stood 11.4 per cent lower at 86.11 dollars, the Financial Times reported, barely 4 per cent above the 83-dollar offering price. heise saw it trading at around 85 dollars later in the day. On Thursday the shares had opened at 111.50 dollars, touched 115.10 and closed at 97.17. The fully diluted valuation has thus shrunk from 1.75 trillion dollars at Thursday's close to about 1.56 trillion.

At the same time the underwriters exercised the greenshoe, an option to sell up to 15 per cent more shares than originally offered. Anthropic had granted the banks 147 million extra shares, which at 83 dollars brings in about 12.2 billion dollars and lifts the IPO proceeds to roughly 93.5 billion. Including a 26-billion-dollar private placement, the company has raised 119.5 billion dollars. "We think that positions us really well," the chief financial officer, Krishna Rao, told Bloomberg. The money is needed: Anthropic posted an operating loss of 567 million dollars in the third quarter, partly because of 5 billion dollars in computing costs. The catch for shareholders is that exercising the option removes the banks' built-in price cushion.

The slide is part of a wider sell-off. Investors fret about debt-funded AI spending, the troubles at Nvidia and the Democratic gains in the midterms, which could make new data centres harder to approve. Chris Beauchamp of IG also sees a self-inflicted effect: investors are selling other stocks to pay for their new Anthropic shares. Demand had been enormous, with the book reportedly at least six times oversubscribed.

History counsels patience rather than panic: Facebook and Uber each lost 11 per cent on their second day, though both then fell further. Cathie Wood's ARK bought shares worth 90.8 million dollars after the debut. The next milestones are a possible Nasdaq-100 inclusion as early as December, quarterly figures in February and, in about 180 days, the end of the insider lock-up.

meldungen.titel: Google makes its Gemini agent free in six countries, but not in Europe
meldungen.text:
Google has opened Tasks in Gemini, the agent previously known as Spark, to free users. Since 17 November the feature, which until now required a paid plan, has been available without charge in the United States, Japan, South Korea, Canada, Australia and India. The agent works through errands on your behalf, from checking bills to comparing prices.

The free tier is narrower than the headlines suggest. The most striking abilities, phone calls to businesses, payments via Google Pay and requests by text message or email, launch only in the United States and only in English. Outside the six countries a paid AI Pro or Ultra plan remains necessary, and according to one report the European Economic Area, the UK and Switzerland are excluded even for subscribers for now.

The move intensifies the race for consumer agents: Google is pushing its assistant into the mass market just as OpenAI, Anthropic and, as job listings revealed this week, Apple are building their own agents that act across apps and the web.

meldungen.titel: Why Claude Code now declines to clone existing games, and the developers who say it goes too far
meldungen.text:
Board game developers are complaining that Claude Code refuses legitimate work, reviving a debate about a rule Anthropic introduced in late October. According to reports, Anthropic added a two-sentence instruction for Claude Code: help with original games, games in an existing genre and users' own designs, but do not recreate a specific existing game, even under a new name. Addy Osmani of Anthropic's technical staff explained that using Claude to infringe intellectual property violates the usage policy.

A developer who builds digital modules of board wargames for paying clients says Claude Code turned that work down; the clients supply the physical games, but the titles are not officially licensed. Several of these refusals, however, appear to stem from Claude Code's cybersecurity safeguards rather than from the game rule. Osmani conceded the change could have unintended consequences and asked developers to report wrongful refusals. Anthropic has not announced a general ban on game development, and original games remain explicitly supported.

Much of the coverage comes from smaller blogs; the most reliable account is Game Developer's reporting, from which Osmani's statement is quoted.

meldungen.titel: A payout every week: what Europe's first weekly-distributing world ETF really delivers
meldungen.text:
Dividend ETFs that pay monthly are old news; now Europe has one that promises to pay every week. The HANetf Weekly World Equity Income UCITS ETF (ISIN IE000I50V6C7) has been tradable on Xetra since 16 September 2026 and is billed as the first ETF in Europe to distribute weekly, with 52 payment dates a year.

The headline figure of around 8 per cent deserves scrutiny. As Finanzwissen points out, it is an indicative projection, not a track record of actual distributions. The payouts so far have been small: 0.0191 dollars per share for the first one, 0.0152 for the most recent, according to one report. Distributions also fluctuate, so the weekly rhythm says nothing about the size or safety of the income.

The broader lesson applies to all distribution products: the frequency of payments changes your cash flow, not your return. What matters is total return after costs and taxes, and every payout counts as taxable income in the year it is received.

meldungen.titel: Black Friday for the AI trade: the Nasdaq wipes out its 2026 gains as the S&P 500 and Dow slide into correction
meldungen.text:
The tech-heavy Nasdaq plunged by more than 4 per cent at times on Friday and erased its entire gain for 2026. The S&P 500 and the Dow Jones slipped into correction territory, more than 10 per cent below their record highs. As recently as early October the Nasdaq was up almost 19 per cent for the year; now it is down nearly 2 per cent, Reuters reported. It is the worst week since the tariff shock of April 2025.

Chipmakers took the heaviest beating. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index fell more than 8 per cent to a seven-month low; Broadcom, AMD and Micron each lost more than 11 per cent. Nvidia dropped about 7 per cent to its lowest since June 2025 and is heading for its longest weekly losing streak since 2008, having shed more than 2.2 trillion dollars of market value since October. The AI cloud providers CoreWeave and Nebius fell more than 10 per cent.

Two forces drive the sell-off. First, growing doubt over whether hundreds of billions spent on data centres will ever pay off; Baird's Michael Antonelli said the notion that AI can keep spending without limit is "ending as we speak". Second, after a hot October inflation reading, markets now price a roughly 98 per cent chance of a Federal Reserve rate rise in December. Add the leadership crisis at Nvidia, whose weight in the indices drags everything with it, and the midterm victories of candidates who want to slow data centre construction.

Yet this is rotation rather than collapse. The ten-year Treasury yield fell from about 5.04 to 4.94 per cent as money fled into bonds; the median S&P 500 stock is still up almost 7 per cent this year, and value stocks could beat growth for the first time since 2022. Strategists such as Antonelli do not think the bull market that began in October 2022 is over. In Vienna, the ATX fell for a seventh consecutive day.

meldungen.titel: Salzburg's valantic Austria buys the Viennese UX agency Liechtenecker
meldungen.text:
valantic Austria, the Salzburg-based Austrian subsidiary of the Munich group valantic, has acquired the Viennese digital agency Liechtenecker. From the start of 2027 the agency will become valantic's Vienna office, with a focus on user experience. The group says it has more than 60 locations in over 20 countries and around 4,300 employees; its Salzburg branch itself grew out of the gradual takeover of the agency elements from 2018 onwards.

Liechtenecker's founder, Susanne Holzer, co-led the agency for almost ten years and has been its sole owner and managing director since 2018. Clients include the Kunsthistorisches Museum in Vienna, Josko, Hilfswerk Österreich and the Austrian Chamber of Pharmacists. Holzer becomes Director UX/CX and head of the Vienna site; the team stays and existing client relationships continue.

valantic Austria wants both a stronger presence in eastern Austria and the Viennese team's expertise in UX research, interface design, usability testing and user-centred product development. Founder and managing director Roland Dessovic speaks of deepening its competence in product strategy. Holzer argues that AI is changing how companies relate to their customers, making customer experience a strategic leadership issue, while managing director Ines Eschbacher insists that even in the AI age "our business remains a people business".
